WASHINGTON Tuesday Oct. 15, 1873
The paying out of silver com to-day by the United States Treasury the most absurd farce that has been seen in Washington for many days. The morning newspapers had announced that they would be put in circulation to-day and the journals in all parts of the country had given the matter much attention for the past week or so; and Banks and bankers from every section had sent orders for large sums. Considerable excitement was created and the Secretary was greatly pleased with his idea. The result of the attempt at least so this city is concerned is ridiculous, and places the Treasury merely on the same foundation as some of the restaurants and places of amusement here when they have been paying out silver in small sums for change for a week or more. Two little bags of silver were placed on the paying clerks' counter on the opening of the cash room, and these were heavily guarded by an ample force of clerks. A circular in plain characters laid on the projecting marble slab told the multitude that creditors of the Government presenting checks or warrants for payment could receive not to exceed $5 of the amount due them in silver coin if they desired. Many men from the Departments and number of citizens went into the cash room during the day to see the long-expected paying out of silver, but the bags on the counter and $10 in silver was all that was seen. It was carefully guarded during the day, however, and the report was carried to Secretary Richardson as the result of inquiries that less than $500 in coin had been paid out as we United States Treasury. This is the result of Mr. Gardner's first attempt to resume specie payments.

THE PUBLIC DEBT INCREASED DURING OCTOBER.

The disbursements by the Treasury Department this month have been heavy and the revenues so light on account of the panic and the unsettled condition of the country that the statement will show an increase, though at present it is not stated to what extent. Should receipts for the remainder of the month keep on the average of past three or four days, the increase of the debt at the end of the month will not be very large. Among the heavy payments this month was one of $650,000 to the Post Office Department for steamship service. There have been other large disbursements; the number of bills presented for settlement exceeded that in any previous month for some time past, while the receipts were from 20 to 15 per cent less. This is accounted for by the fact that nearly all the persons holding claims against the Government came forward for money by claim agents, &c., to procure relief elsewhere. As Secretary Richardson announced early in the panic that he would pay any claims against the Government as rapidly as possible, the creditors took advantage of this means to raise funds of which they would not have wanted in ordinary times.

WORK OF THE SECOND AUDITOR'S OFFICE.

It appears from report of the Second Auditor of the Treasury that the number of accounts examined by him during the past fiscal year was 45,969, of which 8,440 were bounty &c. aggregating over $100,000. Three hundred and ninety-two charges amounting to $72 were raised against officers of the army and volunteers on account of overpayments and double payments, and $5,225 of this sum was recovered and turned into the Treasury. The accounts of 19 paymasters have been balanced, an aggregate of nearly $1,000 having been deposited by them to cancel their indebtedness. United States in nine cases balances were found due the paymasters, the amount paid out on their account being $5,000. The office continues the alert for fraud and fraudulent claims and the Auditor is determined that vigorous prosecution shall follow every detected case. Three hundred and 45 such cases disposed of during the year, and $4,400 recovered. This includes the amount recovered in cases of white soldiers, $5,000; in of colored soldiers principally through the agency of the Freedman's Branch of the Adjutant-General's Office, $685; the amount wrongfully withheld by claim agents and &c., judgments recovered, $1,000. With the continued aid of the officers of the Adjutant-General's Department having charge of the Freedman's Bureau affairs, the Solicitor of the Treasury, and the General practices in the bounty claim business will soon be especially suppressed. The number of cases awaiting action is 449. The letters received during the year number 3,655 and the letters written 2,651, being an increase of 1,851 in the letters received and 1,100 in the letters written.

ECONOMY IN PUBLIC BUILDINGS

Mr. Mullett, supervising Architect of the Treasury Department, in his annual report now preparing, will make one recommendation to Congress that will be received with favor by the taxpayers, not by Congressmen. He will oppose the policy which Congress has adopted within the past two years of voting the public money by hundreds of thousands to public buildings in small out-of-the-way villages and will urge that the Government has all the work that can be done in that line in hand. NEW AND USEFUL INVENTIONS.—Several patents have recently been allowed to Mr. J. N. Baird, of this city, on inventions that promise to be valuable. The absence of Mr. A. Woodward, County Trustee, and the discrepancy discovered in his official accounts, has caused more comment than any similar event in several years. Mr. Woodward was Trustee at the breaking out of the war, and turned over every cent of public money in his hands when the Federals took possession. During the war he made and lost fortune or two in stocks on Wall street, where he doubtless acquired the mania that led to his ruin. He came back poor but respected, and in the spring of 1870 was elected to his old office. At the August election in 1872 he was reelected by large majority in the face of strong party opposition. Each time he gave good bond, and when called upon to exhibit his books to the grand jury he always made a clean balance which defied criticism. The gap, however, through which he evaded the rigid inspection of juries occurred since the first of last January. The law is defective in not requiring county trustees to have their accounts passed oftener than once a year, while other officers settle quarterly and some of them monthly. Since his last settlement the Quarterly Court has issued a large amount of warrants to be cashed by the Trustee. The law requires all warrants so cashed or received for taxes by any other officials to be cancelled from time to time, and stamp is furnished by the county for that purpose. It appears that the warrants cashed by the Trustee have not been cancelled, but since his last settlement were held back and hypothecated on the market for funds with which to speculate in Wall street. The law is severe on this subject, making it a felony to loan, hypothecate or speculate in state or county funds or evidences of indebtedness. Had the Wall street operations proved successful, the warrants put up as collaterals would doubtless have been redeemed, canceled, and turned over as vouchers to the Chairman of the County Court at the end of the year, and the public would have been none the wiser. It is astonishing that man of shrewdness and judgment, or an income of at least eight thousand dollars a year, could be induced by any temptation whatever to take such terrible risk. Such, however, is the force of habit and the ambition to make fortune at a stroke. Hundreds of men have been ruined in the same way, and no warning is sufficient to suppress this great evil of the times. Men are not content to live within their incomes or by the sweat of their brow. They must needs become rich and opulent, and spend money with princely prodigality and keep up with the shoddy ideas of the times. The laws are defective to some extent, and public sentiment is unsound. The world bows down to rich man without inquiring how he become by his money, while the poor, honest mechanic, farmer or laborer is shunned as a thing that blights by its touch and breeds contamination by its presence. Honesty alone is but poor recommendation these times unless backed by powerful influences. Money was the root of all evil in the days of St. Paul, and perhaps will be until the millennium.

HOW THE RASCAL ESCAPED PUNISHMENT.

Messrs. Editors—A struggle for the championship OF this State has been won by a noble hero, single handed, In the town OF Milton, Sussex county, State Of Delaware, BY knocking down a very young lady on the streets OF Milton because the poor girl did not leave the sidewalk and into the street so that this hero might occupy the sidewalk for his lordship. Now this poor girl has been employed by the Delaware Association for the moral improvement and education Of the colored people Of this State, and this hero is also employed to teach In the same town. So you see the occupations of the hero and the poor girl are just the same so far they are both alike, but, sirs, there is a small difference, one is female the other man and hero. There is a greater difference, one is a little darker than the other though the difference is hardly perceptible.

But sirs, the words and conduct of a school teacher—let her be anathema, let her be accursed, and for what? Because she is a school teacher in a colored school and of a darker skin than the hero of this inhuman conduct towards a helpless female. I would recommend this brave man to General W. T. Sherman so that his strong arm and brave heart might render very valuable service in the capture Of the Modocs. Captain Jack, of course, would not be able to offer much resistance to so brave a man as the hero Of the town OF Milton. There is a difference, so renowned, I said, BY those who know, that the teacher Of the colored school is quite comely IN her appearance. This is another cause why she must be struck down by the hand Of this champion Of the ring. It might be proper TO recommend to this boxer that for the benefit OF his pupils he should open a boxing school, so that they may be able to protect themselves from those tender females of the town Of Milton, for they may be in great danger. Now, sirs, this girl and her friends, as I am informed, go TO Georgetown and get a warrant for his arrest. But, sirs, we are disappointed in the officer. He did not serve the warrant In time. So the boxer has ample time TO get a warrant and have this helpless woman bound over under bail for being struck down and beaten in the public streets. Is this the treatment that helpless females are TO receive from the hands of a professedly Christian community? We only ask simple justice at the hands Of a generous public.

CITIZEN.

MCSSELSHELL, August 10.


The abundant preparation. which

meet the savages in the vicinity of
Tongue river has proved correct. The
Indians were discovered for the first

camp at night. No attack TOOK place,

Gustav, with Bloody Knife, and a
squadron of cavalry, had been
detailed by Gen. Stanley TO go and
look up the road. Having got about

ed line OF skirmiSlerS was thrown

vance Of a large party in the neigh
bOrhood, waiting in ambush for the
cavalry. Finding that the ruse failed,
the Indians to the number of 800
boldly rode O4t and advanced on the
grove occupied by the cavalry. Cen
eral Gustav had only n squadron of
50 men, under the command OF Capt.
Mayhem. One body of the troops was
commanded by Lieutenant Gustav,
and the other by Lieutenant Nantum.
The men were again dismounted, and
extended their line in a Seni-cirle
around the cavalry, who had the
river at its back. Rapid firing was
kept up at a distance OF t 0 yards.
While thus engaged with General
CuStar'S front, another party of In
dians crawled along behind, under

ed. The Indians lred the grass in

III capturing the Indians. After three

He then charged the redskins, who

One man wounded in the arm, and

vas going on, several Indians left the
war party, i'll search of StragglerS.
Coming upon DR.. Housinger, our

Private John Ball, of the cavalry,

caml was discovered by the Indians,

Indians. The firing was returned for

dams then crossed the river above

men were disinounted and posted on

The Indians behind the ridges kept
Jap fire until General Gustav ordered
a charge. Our men then mounted
and pursued them boldly for eight
miles. Just at this time the train
came up and opened on the Indians
across the river, with artillery. \. few
shots dispersed them and ended the
fight. This battle, which took place
within two miles of Big Horn, vas a
fierce one. General Gustav and Adju-
toni ketchard had their horses shot
under them. Lieutenant Braden was
badly shot in the thigh. Private Tut
tie. General Custar's orderly, was

The following dispatch was published this morning from the Yellow
stone Expedition

MCCLESKELL, August 10.

The abundant preparation which
the Yellowstone Expedition made
for the resistance of the Indians has
been fully justified. The prediction
of Bloody Knife that we should
meet the savages in the vicinity of
Tongue river has proved correct. The
Indians were discovered for the first
time about August 1st, watching our
movements and prowling around the
camp at night. No attack took place,
however, until August 4th. General
Gustav, with Bloody Knife, and a
squadron of cavalry, had been
detailed by Gen. Stanley to go and
look up the road. Having got about
10 miles ahead, they halted and
picketed their horses in the wood by
the river, to wait for the train. Two
hours afterward six Indians appeared
on the place, and made demonstra-
tions toward their camp. A dismount-
ed line of skirmishers was thrown
out, and the horses saddled. The
Indians were very easily driven
off, but proved to be the advan-
ce of a large party in the neigh-
borhood, waiting in ambush for the
cavalry. Finding that the ruse failed,
the Indians to the number of 800
boldly rode out and advanced on the
grove occupied by the cavalry. Gen-
eral Gustav had only a squadron of
50 men, under the command of Capt.
Mayhem. One body of the troops was
commanded by Lieutenant Gustav,
and the other by Lieutenant Nantum.
The men were again dismounted, and
extended their line in a semi-circle
around the cavalry, who had the
river at its back. Rapid firing was
kept up at a distance of 100 yards.
While thus engaged with General
Custer's front, another party of In-
dians crawled along behind, under
the river bank, and tried to stampede
his horses, but the plan was frustrat-
ed. The Indians fired the grass in
several places, but failed to burn the
cavalry. General Custer deferred a
charge, hoping that the main com-
mando would soon come up and assist
in capturing the Indians. After three
hours fight his ammunition ran out.
He then charged the redskins, who
precipitately fled, dropping many of
their equipments.

One man wounded in the arm, and
one horse wounded, formed the ex-
tent of Custer's loss. While the fight
was going on, several Indians left the
war party, in search of stragglers.
Coming upon Dr. Housinger, our
veterinary surgeon, and Balarain, the
cavalry, who were less than a mile
from the column, they killed them
and took their horses and valuables.

Private John Ball, of the cavalry,
while out hunting, met a similar
fate. In this fight two Indians were
killed, and several ponies taken. On
the 9th of August, four days after the
fight at Tongue river, in the evening,
we came upon the site of the recent
Indian village. Stanley directed
Gustav to take his cavalry, number-
ing 50 men, and follow and punish
the Indians. On the 9th, after a
march of 40 miles, he arrived at the
place where the Indians had crossed
the river, 4 hours before, taking over
their families on rats. Next day he
attempted to cross the Yellowstone,
which at this point is 50 yards wide.
The current was too swift and deep to
swim the horses and men. The at-
tempt to cross he abandoned, for want
of axes and rope. At evening his
camp was discovered by the Indians,
and next morning, the 18th inst, at
daylight, was attacked by about 500
Indians. The firing was returned for
two or three hours, both parties using
trees as a cover. A party of 200 In-
dians then crossed the river above
and below our camp, and endeavored
to gain the bluffs in the rear. Our
men were dismounted and posted on
the bluffs, and received them bravely.
The Indians behind the ridges kept
up fire until General Gustav ordered
a charge. Our men then mounted
and pursued them boldly for eight
miles. Just at this time the train
came up and opened on the Indians
across the river, with artillery. A few
shots dispersed them and ended the
fight. This battle, which took place
within two miles of Big Horn, was a
fierce one. General Gustav and Adju-
tant Ketchard had their horses shot
under them. Lieutenant Braden was
badly shot in the thigh. Private Tut-
tie, General Custer's orderly, was
killed, and 90 of our soldiers were
slightly wounded. We had four
horses killed.

TENNESSEE.

MEMPHIS, August 7.

have assets will find difficulty in con-

verting them into money. This action

of the banks at the clearinghouse meet-

ing gave rise to a feeling of confidence

on the street, that no additional fail-

ures were likely to occur, and the im-

pression obtained that the panic was

over. The leading foreign-exchange

firms, such as Brown Brothers, August

Belmont, and Henry Clews & Co., do

not give any sign of feeling the pressure

of the past three days' crash.

CAUSE OF THE UNION TRUST COMPA-

NY'S FAILURE.

To the too close adherence to the

strict letter of the law by Assistant

Treasurer Hillhouse may be partly

traceable the early suspension of the

Union Trust company. It is under-

stood that the Trust company made a

last offer to the department of a million

five-twenty bonds, desiring therefor a

million dollars in greenbacks, to meet

the fierce drain upon their deposits.

The company assured the department

that as the official hour was twelve

o'clock for offering bonds, this million

should be offered at such figures as would

insure their acceptance by the treasury.

This private offer was not accepted, and

the doors of the Trust company were

closed. Other disasters quickly followed,

and the affairs of the Union Trust COM-

PANY are worse than most people will be

prepared to hear. The amount of

defalcation

is larger than at first supposed. It is

said it will exceed five hundred thous-

and dollars. The directors are

considering the question of appointing a

receiver. Carleton has been traced to

two or three different hotels in town,

or into Jersey City, from whence he

took the train of the New Jersey Cen-

tral railway last evening. The directors

have made no effort to secure him; the

efforts made to trace his whereabouts

have been made by private individuals.

A member of the governing committee

of the stock gave it as his opinion, when

questioned, that

PUBLIC CONFIDENCE WAS RETURNING

this morning, and the excitement would

have died away without further serious

disaster but for the suspension of the

Union Trust company.

By the time the doors of the First

National bank of Hoboken had opened

this morning about fifty depositors had

assembled to demand their money. The

tellers went to work and closed accounts

as rapidly as possible. The crowd mean-

while increased in size, until not less

than one hundred and fifty depositors

were awaiting their turn. The deposi-

tors are making arrangements to hold

a meeting early in the week. It is said

that of two hundred and seven thousand

dollars which the bank has on deposit

in New York a large share was in the

hands of the bank of Commonwealth.

SPRAGUE NOT A DEFAULTER.

NEW YORK, September 20.—It was

rumored this afternoon that a large

amount of city funds is deposited in one

of the suspended banks, and that some

county funds were with the Union Trust

company. Counsel for Ex-City Treas-

urer Sprague, of Brooklyn, has sent the

following letter to the comptroller of that

city. It is apparent that neither

Sprague nor Rodman is a defaulter to the

city. You are required to take notice of

this fact. You will not therefore make

any disposition of any of the property

transferred to you by Mr. Sprague, as he

was deceived and in error. In that re-

spect, the comptroller says for the

present he will retain the property.

ALL RIGHT AT THE HUB.

BOSTON, September 20.—The financial

alarm in New York is the principal top-

ic of conversation, but so far does not in-

terfere with business.

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the State of Louisiana in General Assembly convened, That in case of refusal or when property is assessed, to pay the taxes thereon within ten days after the expiration of the public notice required by law, the tax collectors may give ten days written or printed notice to the owner or agent of the property assessed to pay said tax, after which delay, if not fully paid, the said tax collector may make a seizure of such property by recording a description of the same with the amount due in the mortgage book of the parish where it is situated, and on the fourth day of such recording shall proceed to sell said property without legal process to pay said tax and all lawful costs, after advertising three times within ten days in the official journal, and in the country parishes where such publications cannot be made by public notice for such ten days provided, that when personal property sufficient in amount is found to satisfy the State's claim against such taxpayer, the same shall be seized to satisfy such claims in preference to real estate. The tax collector may, if necessary, bring suit and have other due judicial processes in the name of the State provided, that in all such cases he be represented by the law officer of the State.


Sec. 2. Be it further enacted, etc.,
That in all cases of neglect or refusal to pay their licenses, of any description, by any person, firm, company or corporation doing business in this State, the tax collector shall give ten days written or printed notice to such delinquent taxpayer to pay such licenses, if such delinquent can be found; otherwise the notice shall be given by publication for ten days in the official journal, if there be one in the parish; if there be no official journal published in the parish, the notice may be posted at the courthouse door, and if at the expiration of said notice the license, together with the costs, be not fully paid, the tax collector may, without any judicial formality, proceed to seize and sell, after ten days advertisement, the property, rights and credits of such delinquent taxpayer, or so much thereof as may be necessary to satisfy the claims of the State, as aforesaid, together with all legal costs and charges. The tax collector may, when represented by the proper law officer of the State, obtain from any court of competent jurisdiction, in the name of the State, a writ of Injunction against any person who may not have paid his license, restraining any such person from pursuing his business or calling until such license is paid. In such cases the court shall render Judgment for the amount of the license due, with twenty per cent special damages. In the parish of Orleans all suits for licenses and other taxes, State or municipal, shall, whatever amount, be brought before the Superior District Court.


SEC. 3. Be it further enacted, ETC.,

That all causes which may be commenced hereafter in any of the courts in this State, in which it is sought to enjoin or delay the collection of any licenses or taxes whatever, whether State or parish, general or special imposed by competent authority, shall be regarded as preference cases, and the court shall proceed to final trial and determination of the same at the earliest moment compatible with the ends of justice and tax collectors shall not be liable for damages for prosecuting such cases, and upon a dissolution of any Injunction hereafter granted to enjoin or delay the collection of any such taxes so levied or imposed upon any person or property in this State the court ordering such injunction to be dissolved shall enter a decree against the person or persons suing out the same and his or their securities on their injunction bond for the sum of one hundred per centum on the amount of all taxes, the collections of which was delayed or enjoined, and all costs of suit and said DECREES shall be enforced as other DECREES are enforced, and then collected and paid into the proper treasury.

That the tax collectors shall be and are hereby authorized to give a title in the name of the State of Louisiana to all persons purchasing property sold in pursuance of this act, and such title shall be held in and recognized by all courts of this State as valid in law, for which it shall the tax collector shall be allowed a fee of two dollars; upon the presentation of a title so given to the district court Judge to order the sheriff to put such persons in possession of the property so purchased by him.

Since the treaty of Fontainebleau in 1853 when
the island was ceded to Great Britain by the
French, the immigration has progressed by no
small measure. The length of the island is 100 miles and the breadth
about thirty-four miles. The standing grievance
for the last ninety years has been the land ques-
tion owing to the plan then adopted for its distri-
bution. The great object of the majority of the people is to settle
with the least trouble and expenses. Much has since
been done to purchase fine estates of large non-
resident proprietors, who did little or nothing to
the island. Several fertile tracts have
been sold in retail to the tenant, and the result
is a prosperous one. Many of the farmers in the agricu-

the centenarians throughout the country speak of
it in the highest terms and, if I mistake not, Sum-
merside and other kindred localities will make
famous watering places for over-heated Canadians;

summer residence delightful. But it is in the
soil that the island excels. It is strong and rich to a uniformly un-
common degree. There is no portion of the lower
island with better prospects of good return than in this
soil. Such, indeed, is the excellence of the soil
that good crops are produced immediately upon it. It is
well adapted to the growth of wheat, oats and
potatoes, of which large quantities are annually
produced, while the specimens of live stock that have seen
the light of day at different points would carry prizes at a wen-

are raised in Prince Edward Island.

Any boy five years old here who fails to pin his
lobster on the first dab is supposed to be a dis-
grace to his family. To see the quantities of fish
in indifference with which the amateur hooks
his two and three hundred sea trout;
the thousands of mackerel dancing fam-
ously in well protected nets; the majestic salmon
looking like so many heroic but crestfallen conquerors
under the regiments of inflated halibut; loads of
cod and unfortunate herring, all lying near
a relentless enemy, is enough to suggest a
feeling, not exactly of commiseration but of comedy;

the fish. I am told that the walrus was wont to
frequent the shores in large numbers, and was a
source of considerable profit, but of late years that

these promising features, however, there is deci-

island, and there is no doubt that the new condi-

government has administered the laws. The
Legislature consists of a Governor, who is ap-

a hotel in the place. At Summerside, however, a fine
edifice is in course of construction and as it is the
first of its kind the island will no doubt other rival
establishments will be commenced.

for terms, there is every hope that now, the bar-
rier to progress having been removed, they will
step into the van of the Dominion and proceed at
a lively and interesting pace that has hitherto
marked that broad domain.

The Times of the same date gives the latest facts and concludes with what may possibly prove a clue to the identity of the murdered woman.

NEW YORK, April 21st.—The recovery of nearly
a quarter of million dollars in U. S. bonds, which
had been obtained by McDonald, alias Bidwell and
associates in the late Bank of England forgeries was
effected to-day. The facts concerning the recovery
are as follows:


On the 9th of March last, a trunk said to contain
wearing apparel, old and in use, was delivered at the
office of the North Atlantic Express Company, No. 4
Margaret street, London, by a person calling him-
self C. Leasing, of Tunbridge Wells, England, and
addressed to Major George Mathews, New York, to
be kept in bond at the express office No. 11 Broad
way, New York, until called for. The trunk was du-
ly forwarded by the express company and reached
New York by the steamship Cuba, which arrived
March 10th, and was kept in bond by the company
as per instructions, until Saturday last, when a wo-
man calling herself Mrs. George Mathews presented
an order for its delivery at the express office duly
signed George Mathews. In the meantime the coun-
sel for the Bank of England had received infor-
mation with regard to the trunk which led to its de-
tention by the company until to-day, when it was
taken possession of under an order of the Supreme
Court by Nathaniel Jarvis, Receiver in the Bank of
England forgery case, and being opened and ex-

linen, amounting in all to $220,905. The bonds were

The annual meeting of the Association of Medical Superintendents of American Institutions for the Insane commenced at the Ewell House, in Baltimore, on Tuesday. The Association numbers nearly one hundred members, from all sections of the Union, and embraces Canada. About forty-five members were present yesterday. The meeting is held in a room in The hotel, where its sessions took place twenty years ago; since which time it has not met in Baltimore until now. There are thirteen men living who then belonged to the Association, five of whom were present on this occasion.

Drs. Striking and Conrad, of Virginia, and Dr. Fuller, of North Carolina, were among the members in attendance.

Dr. John J. Butler president, Dr. F. W. Nichols vice-president, and Dr. John Carwen, secretary.

The morning session was principally devoted to the discussion of the general care of the insane, under three classes: the colored class, the criminal class, and the epileptic and imbecile class. The points discussed were whether insane criminals should be treated in special hospitals or retained, as they generally now are, in public hospitals, among ordinary patients; the increase of insanity among the colored population, and the general movement for the care of the insane in the States under legislative action. The questions were ably discussed by Dr. Smart, Dr. Green, Dr. Earle, Dr. Gray, Dr. Walker, Dr. Calender, Dr. Tyler, Dr. Nichols, and Dr. Stribling.

It was argued that special hospitals or separate apartments should be erected in connection with State hospitals and prisons for such persons. In this connection it was argued by Dr. Tyler that there was a liability of a relapse of the disease, hence it was a very important point in jurisprudence as to how long should be the confinement of insane criminals after apparent recovery of the person so confined. It was shown by some of the speakers that there was recently an increase of insanity among the colored people.

Dr. Stribling discussed particularly the provisions that should be made for colored insane persons. His version of the law in Virginia in the time slavery existed was that institutions were not obliged to care for the colored class; that each shareholder was to care for his own insane of that class. The speaker had advocated before the Virginia Legislature that there should be separate institutions or separate buildings for the colored insane. Insanity among the colored class in Virginia, he said, was greatly on the increase. In the time of slavery he did not think there were over fifty insane colored people in the State. Now, he thought, the census would show that there were three or four hundred.

It was shown during the discussion that there was steady increase in the sympathy manifested by the public for the care of the insane, and more liberal appropriations for the founding of insane institutions were being made. It was argued that persons who commit murder while insane, and were therefore dangerous, should be confined separately, so as not to disturb others who were peaceably disposed and quiet in their demeanor.

The President appointed Drs. Tyler, Stribling, and Barlow as a committee to nominate officers of the Association, and in advance of the nominations announced his resignation as presiding officer, after thanking the Association for the kindness, forbearance, &c., extended him.

Bah! they are afraid of getting their labor-
ers' hands muddy. I will undertake to put
a gang of men down there with nothing
but crowbars in their hands, who will lift
that gate up, put the rollers under and push
it back in two hours. Then you see the
water lying there. Well, we have been al-
ready to go out since last Monday, but they
said they couldn't get that water out. That
is all nonsense. They have not been try-
ing to get the water out. They have only got
that little donkey engine at work, and even
that stops work at half-past four o'clock
and as much water leaks in every night as
they pump out in the day time. They have
got here a splendid steam engine built at
West Point, which would take that water
out in four hours, but they haven't been in
any hurry to get it out. That dodge lasted
eight days, and then, when they found it
wouldn't last any longer, what did they do?
Why, in the dead of night, at a time when
all honest men ought to be in bed, they
scuttled a barge which they had brought
right up in front of the dock, and sunk it
right in our way."


"But don't you suppose the barge was
sunk accidentally?"


AN EXASPERATED SPANISH OFFICER.


At this question the officer became very
much excited. He jumped up and down in
his anger, and scowled, stamped, and swore
as he thought of it, finally managing to
calculate: "Oh, my God, how can you
ask me such a question? You know it was no
accident. Sacramento! How could it be
an accident? There was nobody on the boat.
There was nobody near the boat when she
went down. It was not an accident. It is
part of their game. I myself heard one of
their men say two weeks ago, 'The Ara-
piles is not gone yet, and the Arapiles will
not go until we get the Virginius back.'


Now, is that courtesy? Is that fair treat-
ment of us? We are not at war, and they
have nothing to do with us, except to use
the use of their dock, which we pay for
like any other customer, and let us go in.
We want to go. We are at war, don't you
know, how much fight we have; but that is
the way the Americans fight. Bah! I shall
tell you what the Arapiles will do if she is
given a chance to capture the Gloucester!"
"Yes, what will she do?"


"She won't capture her. She will run
her down. No more capture—no more—
ever!"


The officer again became somewhat calm
and went in as follows:


"INSULTS AND ABUSE."
"They say the Arapiles is the guest
of the United States. This is a nice way
to treat a guest, isn't it? She is a very good
customer. We pay for everything, and we
have spent since we have been here
between eighty and ninety thousand dollars.
This is all abuse and insults and
abuses and insults. We have invited an
American officer on board of our vessel, and
he has used us to a hoard and abused us
greatly. Do they always behave this way?
No, of course not. They are always
insulting and abusing."

pleasant little affairs in which it has
ever been our lot to participate was a
veritable surprise party at the resi-
dence of Mrs. Andrew Gingry, corner
of Railroad Avenue and Claiborne
street, Wednesday night. The per-
sons for whom the surprise was in
tended-being some young ladies from
Baton Rouge who are here on a visit
to relatives-were kept in profound
ignorance of the intended event, the
first intimation of its occurrence they
received being the sudden appearance
at the house Of quite a numerous par
ty of young ladies and gentlemen, a
majority Of the latter members of the
Ascension Brass Band. The parlors
and spacious hall were cleared of fur
niture, and in half hour the music
Of the Ascension String Band was re-
sounding and the dancing had begun.
What with music, dancing, singing,
chatting, eating cake, drinking lem
onade and milk punch, ETC., the time
passed SO rapidly and pleasantly by
that no one took note Of the feeting
hours or became weary, and it was
almost daybreak when the festivities
came to close and the guests de-
parted for their homes. Of all pres
ent, none seemed to enjoy the affair
with greater zest than the young Ia
dies in whose honor the entertainment
was projected. Mrs. Gingry and her
son, Andrew j. Gingry, Esq, exerted
themselves most successfully to make
the guests comfortable, and to their
efforts were due in great degree the
perfect harmony Of the occasion. The
pleasant little surprise party was a
complete success, and we shall not be
astonished to hear Of another of the
same sort occurring at somebody else's
house ere many weeks have come and
gone.
